subject: english
title: Ab：語音

content.summary: 本課以重音、節奏、連音、停頓與語調理解英文口語如何傳遞意思；例句、對話與錄音任務均為本課自編。

sections.heading: 學習目標
sections.body: 能在字詞、句子與對話層次辨識重音、節奏、停頓及語調，並以溝通目的解釋其作用。

sections.heading: 學習流程
sections.body: 先確認說話者、受話者與目的，再標記聽到的聲音線索，最後用語境和聽者回應檢查解釋是否合理。

sections.heading: 常見錯誤
sections.body: 不要把拼字直接當成發音，也不要把某一種口音當成唯一標準；要區分聽到的線索、推測的態度與仍缺少的語境。

sections.heading: 自我檢核
sections.body: 在新對話中選擇一項重音或語調調整，說明它如何幫助聽者理解，並指出一項證據限制。

studyHighlights: 先判斷說話目的，再辨認重音、節奏、停頓和語調如何改變聽者理解。
用原創句子錄音或朗讀，比較聲音特徵與語境，不把拼字當成完整發音規則。
用聽者能否重述重點檢查溝通效果，並標出錄音或語境不足的限制。

body.heading: When a message sounds different, meaning can change
body.body: Imagine a student saying, “You finished the project.” The words may be a question, a surprised response, or a plain statement depending on the voice. Begin by listening for the final pitch, the strongest word, pauses, and the number of beats in the sentence. Do not treat pronunciation as decoration: sound carries grammar, attitude, and the listener’s attention. In this unit, you will compare a spoken line with its written form, mark what you hear, and explain which sound clue supports your interpretation. The first task is not to imitate a perfect accent; it is to notice a sound choice and connect it to a communicative purpose.

body.heading: Three layers of spoken English
body.body: English pronunciation becomes easier to understand when three layers are kept apart. At the word level, syllables have stressed and unstressed beats, and a vowel may change when the stress changes. At the sentence level, important information usually receives more prominence, while grammar words may be shorter and weaker. At the discourse level, rising or falling intonation helps signal whether a speaker is checking, finishing, listing, or showing an attitude. Spelling is useful evidence but not a complete sound map: words such as “record” can shift stress when they change grammatical role, and connected speech can make a written boundary less obvious. Your goal is to choose a sound feature that fits the context rather than to guess from letters alone.

body.heading: A small listening investigation
body.body: Use the original pair “You sent the file.” and “You sent the file?” First read both lines silently, then predict how the final pitch might differ. Next, mark the stressed word in three versions: YOU sent the file, You SENT the file, and You sent the FILE. The words stay the same, but the contrast changes the implied correction: perhaps someone else did it, the action was sending, or the file—not a message—was sent. Finally, read the line at a natural pace and record whether your pause, stress, and pitch match the intended context. This example shows why a pronunciation answer needs a communicative reason, not merely a phonetic label.

body.heading: Build a sound-and-meaning record
body.body: Choose a short classroom dialogue and make four columns: written sentence, stressed item, intonation or pause, and meaning in the situation. Read the first line without changing its rhythm. On the second reading, move the stress to a different content word and ask a partner what contrast they hear. Then practise a question, a list, and a finished statement; use a rising contour for a genuine check and a falling contour when the thought is complete, while remembering that speakers may vary. If a partner cannot hear your intended contrast, revise one feature at a time. Do not score yourself by resemblance to one speaker. Score whether another listener can recover the intended meaning from your evidence.

body.heading: Transfer the skill to real communication
body.body: Apply the same listening choices to a school announcement, a café order, and a group-project discussion. In an announcement, pauses can separate instructions; in an order, final rising pitch may invite confirmation; in a discussion, sentence stress can politely highlight a different priority. Before speaking, identify audience, purpose, and the one idea that must be heard. After speaking, ask the listener to repeat the key information rather than asking whether your accent sounds native. If the listener misunderstood, check vocabulary, word order, stress, speed, and background noise separately. Clear communication is a design problem with several possible solutions, not a single imitation test.

body.heading: Reflect on what the listener actually received
body.body: Finish by replaying one recording or rereading one dialogue with three questions. Which syllable or word carried the contrast? Which pause, rhythm, or pitch helped the listener predict the speaker’s intention? What could not be decided because the recording was too short, the context was missing, or speakers naturally used different varieties of English? Write a short reflection such as, “I stressed FILE to correct the object, and my partner identified the contrast; I still need a fuller context to judge the speaker’s attitude.” This keeps pronunciation, interpretation, and evidence connected. A successful learner can adjust a sound choice for a purpose and can also state the limit of what the sound alone proves.
